title: Thornton Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Thornton wells have a 42-foot median depth, but some reach 1,581 feet. See yields, water levels, permits, risks and drilling costs.
h1: What Thornton Well Records Tell You Before You Buy
intro_html:
Thornton sits on the plains, but well conditions vary more than the flat ground suggests. Records within 5 miles show a median well depth of 42 feet, while the middle half runs from 25 to 350 feet. That wide spread matters when you are pricing a new well or evaluating an existing one.

Most records are tied to Denver Basin aquifers, with many permits identifying unnamed or fractured-bedrock conditions. The database includes domestic, irrigation and monitoring wells, so it is not a perfect picture of household wells alone. Use these results to set expectations, then verify the permit, construction report, pump test and water quality for the specific property.

sections.heading: Thornton well depths range from shallow to very deep
sections.html:
The typical recorded depth near Thornton is shallow: the median is 42 feet, and 64% of wells are under 100 feet. That does not mean every lot can be served by a shallow well. The middle half of reported depths extends from 25 to 350 feet, 19% are between 300 and 600 feet, and 10% exceed 600 feet. The deepest record is 1,581 feet.

For a drilling bid, the median is only a starting reference. A site with nearby shallow wells may still encounter different sediments, bedrock or water-bearing zones. Review neighboring construction reports near Northglenn, Henderson and Welby, but do not treat one nearby depth as a guarantee. The aquifer label and the actual well logs are more useful than distance alone.

sections.heading: What a Thornton well may produce
sections.html:
Among the wells that report a pump yield, the median is 12.0 gallons per minute. The middle half falls between 10.0 and 15.0 gallons per minute. That is a solid planning range for many household uses, but yield reports cover only 513 wells, so the result is not a guarantee for every parcel.

Low production is uncommon in these records: 0% report under 1 gallon per minute, 3% report 1 to 5 gallons per minute, 59% report 5 to 15 gallons per minute, and 39% report more than 15 gallons per minute. Ask for the well completion report and pump test. Storage capacity, pressure equipment and the permitted use still matter, especially when irrigation or livestock is part of the plan.

sections.heading: Thornton water levels are relatively shallow in the records
sections.html:
The median static water level is 14 feet below ground surface, with the middle half between 9 and 35 feet. These measurements come from 209 wells, far fewer than the total permit records, and static level is not the same as the water available while pumping. Seasonal conditions and nearby pumping can change the reading.

The decade pattern does not show a simple ongoing drop. The median was 24 feet below surface in the 2000s, 11 feet in the 2010s and 13 feet in the 2020s. The more recent figures are shallower than the 2000s, with the 2020s slightly deeper than the 2010s. Treat that as a record-based snapshot, not a guarantee of future water levels at a particular home.

sections.heading: Permit history points to long-term drilling activity
sections.html:
Colorado DWR records contain 4,832 permitted wells within the mapped area, including 2,597 recorded as constructed. Permit activity increased from 178 permits in the 1950s to 856 in the 2000s, then totaled 664 in the 2010s and 483 in the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025.

The use mix is not all residential: 34% are domestic or household, 9% irrigation, 4% stock and 39% monitoring. The most active names in the records are Authorized (Pe, Pg), John'S Drilling Inc. (John, Lloyd), and Roger Schocke Well Drlg. Inc. (Schocke, Roger). Confirm the current license, scope and references before selecting a driller.

sections.heading: Thornton drilling cost depends on the finished system
sections.html:
The cost model for Thornton uses Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock and a drilling rate of $50 to $70 per foot. At the recorded median depth of 42 feet, the drilled hole is estimated at about $2,100 to $2,900. That is only the hole, not a functioning water system.

A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching and electrical is modeled at about $8,100 to $14,900 at that depth. Deeper drilling, difficult access, casing and grout requirements, water treatment, rock conditions or longer utility runs can change the bid. Get a written proposal that separates drilling from casing, grout, pump equipment, trenching, electrical and testing. A shallow median should not be used as a fixed price for a particular lot.

sections.heading: Check water quality, dry-hole risk and building constraints
sections.html:
Environmental review deserves attention around Thornton. The mapped area within about 10 miles includes 714 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 44 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites and 24 historic mine features. Those mapped sites do not prove a problem at a specific address, but they are a reason to test the well and review nearby land uses before closing.

Low yield and dry holes remain site-specific risks despite the reported production numbers. Check well construction, casing, grout, pump test results and maintenance history. For a new build, confirm the permitted use, septic setbacks, soil conditions, access for a rig and space for replacement equipment. A well permit does not by itself guarantee safe water, adequate supply or approval for every intended use.

sections.heading: Use nearby wells to price and plan a Thornton lot
sections.html:
Before buying, pull the DWR records for the parcel and the closest completed wells. Compare depth, aquifer description, construction, static water level and reported yield rather than relying on the neighborhood average. Properties near Federal Heights, Todd Creek and Derby may provide useful context, but local geology can change over short distances.

For a new well, confirm the permit pathway before excavation. Household-use wells may be exempt wells, while a proposed irrigation or other use can involve different limits and requirements. In an over-appropriated basin, an augmentation plan may be needed. Have a driller and septic professional review access, setbacks, pump sizing and water storage before you finalize a purchase or house layout.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Thornton, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within 5 miles of Thornton is 42 feet. The middle half of wells ranges from 25 to 350 feet, so the local spread is wide. About 64% are under 100 feet, while 10% exceed 600 feet. The deepest recorded well is 1,581 feet.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Thornton?
faq.a: The local cost model uses $50 to $70 per foot. At the 42-foot median depth, drilling the hole is estimated at about $2,100 to $2,900. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is estimated at about $8,100 to $14,900. Greater depth, access and site conditions can increase the bid.

faq.q: How much water does a Thornton well produce?
faq.a: Reported pump yield has a median of 12.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 10.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. About 59% of reported wells produce 5 to 15 gallons per minute and 39% produce more than 15. These figures cover 513 reported yields, so request the specific well's test.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Thornton?
faq.a: The records do not establish that a particular Thornton well is safe to drink. Within about 10 miles, mapping shows 714 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 44 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test the property well through a qualified laboratory and review nearby environmental records before using the water for drinking.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping in Thornton?
faq.a: The available decade figures do not show a simple ongoing drop. Median static water level was 24 feet below surface in the 2000s, 11 feet in the 2010s and 13 feet in the 2020s. The sample includes 209 reported measurements, and static levels vary by location, season and pumping, so it is not a guarantee for a specific lot.
